topic: Why did the Tacoma Narrows Bridge tear itself apart in the wind?
research_summary: Candidates (scored /40, 20 Nov 2026): (1) Why did the Tacoma Narrows Bridge tear itself apart in the wind? (Earth & Nature, cooling-adjacent) 28 - kept as follow-up; (4) Why do fireflies flash in sync with no conductor? Research (web search, each fact cross-checked against at least two independent sources): the bridge opened to traffic 1 July 1940 and collapsed 7 November 1940, about four months later, VERIFIED (multiple independent news/engineering retrospectives agree on both dates); wind that morning was about 40 mph / 64 km/h, a moderate, unremarkable wind for a bridge of that size, VERIFIED (contemporary measurement figures, consistent across sources, though exact instantaneous readings vary slightly 38-42 mph); the popular explanation that simple mechanical 'resonance' (like an opera singer shattering a glass) brought it down is a known oversimplification - modern engineering sources and a 2022 Journal of Fluid Mechanics study describe the real mechanism as aeroelastic flutter, a self-reinforcing feedback loop where the bridge's own twisting motion changed the airflow around it, which fed more energy back into the twisting, VERIFIED; the deck used solid plate girders (about 2.4 m deep) instead of open trusses, so it caught the wind like a sail/wing - contrasted explicitly with the Golden Gate Bridge's open-truss design in engineering retrospectives, VERIFIED; no human died in the collapse - the only casualty was a dog, Tubby, left in an abandoned car; Professor Farquharson tried to rescue him, was bitten, and escaped the span moments before that section fell, VERIFIED (multiple independent retrospectives, including ASCE's own history page, agree); the collapse was filmed on 16mm Kodachrome by Barney Elliott and Harbine Monroe and is famous enough to have been added to the US National Film Registry in 1998, VERIFIED; the replacement bridge (1950) used open trusses and wind-tunnel-tested aerodynamics, now standard practice for long-span suspension bridges, VERIFIED (consistent across engineering sources, though I treat the specific claim 'could 1940 engineers have predicted this' as an open, debated question rather than a settled fact - framed as a question for the viewer, not asserted). scenes.text: A brand-new bridge once swayed so hard it tore itself apart. Why?
This happened in 1940, only four months after the bridge opened to traffic.
The wind that morning was only about 64 kilometers an hour, barely a strong breeze.
So was this just resonance, like a singer shattering a glass? Not quite.
The wind kept pumping energy into the bridge's own twisting motion until it grew out of control.
Why did it fail at all? The deck was solid steel plate, built thin to save money, so wind pushed it like a sail.
Engineers rebuilt it with open trusses and wind-tunnel testing, now standard on every big bridge. Do you think the first builders could have caught this?

scenes.text: एक बिल्कुल नया पुल इतनी ज़ोर से हिला कि वह खुद ही टूट गया। आखिर क्यों?
यह 1940 में हुआ, पुल खुलने के सिर्फ चार महीने बाद।
उस सुबह हवा की रफ़्तार लगभग 64 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटा थी, बस एक सामान्य हवा।
तो क्या यह सिर्फ अनुनाद था, जैसे गायक गिलास तोड़ देता है? बिल्कुल नहीं।
हवा पुल की अपनी मरोड़ में लगातार ऊर्जा भरती गई, जब तक यह काबू से बाहर न हो गई।
यह फेल क्यों हुआ? डेक ठोस स्टील प्लेट का था, पैसे बचाने के लिए पतला बनाया गया, तो हवा उसे पाल की तरह धकेलती रही।
इंजीनियरों ने इसे खुले ढांचे और पवन-सुरंग परीक्षण से दोबारा बनाया, जो अब हर बड़े पुल में आम है। क्या तुम्हें लगता है पहले इंजीनियर यह भांप सकते थे?
